turns.prompt_text: I've been having this idea in my mind that if there's something really good to be made, people will make it. But I've been countering that argument lately that there's a lot of localization and my local problems will be not will not be solved elsewhere. They will be solved by me or people in my direct situation. But other than that other people are not really able to solve my problems Sometimes other people solve tangentially related problems and that's really cool but I then have to transport that into a way I can use I've been specifically thinking about this in terms of AI cuz there's a lot of people experimenting with it, but I don't think that the things other people make aren't necessarily going to be the best for me Because it's like designing my own third arm. I know how I'm going to use it. Other people don't
turns.response_html:
That "third arm" analogy is spot on. A corporation designing a third arm for the mass market is going to build a generic gripper—something that sort of helps the average person hold a grocery bag, but doesn't actually help you execute the highly specific tasks you do every day.

The idea that "if it's worth making, someone else will make it" assumes that value is universal. But as you're realizing, value is deeply localized.

The "Lowest Common Denominator" Problem

When developers build mass-market tools—especially in the current AI boom—they are economically incentivized to solve the 80% of a problem that applies to the most people. They aren't going to build the final 20% that caters exclusively to your specific decentralized data structures, your local hardware environment, or your exact workflow preferences.

Waiting for the market to solve your highly specific, localized problems means you will always be waiting.

The Friction of Translation

You hit on a crucial pain point: the translation tax. When you find a tangentially related tool, you have to spend energy stripping away the assumptions the original creator made, reverse-engineering their logic, and jury-rigging it to fit your actual need.

Sometimes, the effort required to adapt a generalized, off-the-shelf Python wrapper into a localized solution takes more energy than just building a custom autonomous execution loop from scratch in a language that gives you total control. You end up fighting the tool's intended design rather than solving your own problem.

Bespoke Systems

With AI, we are shifting from an era where we all had to adapt our workflows to fit generic software, into an era where we can build bespoke intelligence layers.

When you design your own agentic frameworks or even your own parametric physical mechanisms, you aren't just making a tool; you're encoding your personal leverage. You know exactly what inputs you care about, exactly what kind of friction you want to eliminate, and exactly how the output needs to look.

No one else has that context. No one else can build your third arm.
